title: AC Circuits — RMS, Impedance & Power Factor
subtitle: AC circuits are the backbone of power systems. R, L, C behave very differently in AC. Impedance and power factor are the two concepts that unlock everything. The RMS value is what actually matters for power calculations.
learningOutcome: AC circuits are the backbone of power systems. R, L, C behave very differently in AC. Impedance and power factor are the two concepts that unlock everything. The RMS value is what actually matters for power calculations.

content.text: AC voltage: e(t) = Eₘsin(ωt+φ). RMS = Eₘ/√2 = 0.707Eₘ — DC equivalent for same average power. "230V mains" = 230V RMS; actual peak = 325V. Average (half-cycle) = 0.637Eₘ.

R: opposes at all frequencies, V and I in phase. XL = 2πfL — increases with f, voltage leads current 90°. XC = 1/(2πfC) — decreases with f, current leads voltage 90°. Total impedance Z = √(R²+X²), V = IZ.

Power factor cosφ = R/Z = P/S. Lagging = inductive load. Leading = capacitive load. Low PF → more current needed for same real power → more I²R line losses. Utilities penalise industrial customers for low PF.

Common mistake — The most common AC mistake Adding VR + VL directly: 159+166.5=325.5V ≠ 230V. You CANNOT add out-of-phase AC voltages arithmetically. They are 90° apart — use Pythagoras: V = √(VR²+VL²). This costs marks in almost every exam cohort.
